source_text:
Do you have a fully mechanical strategy with set rules that you follow each day without really having to think about it or do you trade more price action based/discretionary?
I wonder how many people have been able to create a fully mechanical strategy that’s profitable or that there’s always some discretion involved if you want to be profitable. My goal is to get to something fully mechanical but I don’t know how realistic that is
Actually, I have some hard rules, but they are not enough, if there are some fundamental reasons or other for doing nothing, I do nothing. If I traded mechanically technically, I would be trading too much.
Sort of.

I have set ups. I see them appear, my signals say it’s time to get ready. Wait for decent location.

Then I enter.

I leave the room after that and set an alert to tell me when the trades done. Pretty much it now.
"set it and forget it" does not exist, imho.   
  
As a discretionary trader that wants to start automating trades, I have to accept the fact that one thing for certain is that there will always change. In markets, regimes, life. So yes we have cycles where a strategy will work, but where traders (myself included) get hurt is we try to force a strategy that once crushed, and no longer does because momentum died down or reason XYZ.
The thing about systematic trading is that you don’t actually want the market to work that way. If your trading style is completely systematic with no discretionary input, that means the edge is *razor* thin. As soon as even *one* variable in the market changes, it could throw your entire system off.

On the other hand, how could a market maker possibly arbitrage away a discretionary trader’s style? There are too many variables. The trader might not even be able to articulate why they did what they did. It’s about skill, responsiveness, reaction time, and intuition.
yes and even then you have to put in other deterministic checks even with backtesters like VBT and Nautilus trader so the LLM doesn't try to bypass them.
I don't think it's possible. Even institutions who mostly use algos in their trading need to modify their algos every now and then to keep up with different market conditions. Discretionary trading is the way to go.
fully mechanical is realistic, but be ready for what it shows you. once every rule is written down and backtested, there's nowhere to  
  hide. a lot of strategies that feel great when traded by feel turn out to have a much thinner edge than you thought, or none. with  
  discretion you never find that out, you just remember the good calls.

  easiest way to start is writing down the decisions you already make by feel, one rule at a time. "I don't take trades in the first 15  
  min", "I skip if spread is above X". after a while most of your discretion turns out to be rules you hadn't written yet.
I think fully mechanical is realistic for entries and stops, and most of the discretion left over is just whether you actually follow it. If you want to check that, I use and run Tradervana, and you can list your strategy steps so each trade asks which ones you followed, so after a month you can see whether the losers came from the rules or from going off script. What made my rules stick was proving them out first, because once I trusted the setup every trade felt like just another trade and the FOMO mostly went away.
What do you trade it on, Nq, 9.30am? What tf is your entry on, where is your SL and what RR do you aim for pls?
I have a strategy with 13 rules.  It works. It’s great.  I just don’t have the discipline to follow it.  I would actually be up millions if I followed it.
Is anyone using Tommaso Sillian’s method? The 2 Hour Futures Trader.
I think there's a difference between having mechanical rules and having a fully automated strategy. You can have very specific entry conditions, fixed risk, max trades per day, and rules for when you're not allowed to trade without having a bot place orders for you. There are journals and discipline tracking tools that can help you monitor whether you're actually following those rules too. The biggest thing I'd want to know is whether the strategy works when you follow it exactly, or whether you're constantly making exceptions. That's where the data gets interesting.
that sounds smart, im going to work on a project for that
> Do you apply the "veto" idea to your exits at all or is it just for entries? For example, holding the position for a higher ATR multiple when the narrative for the trade idea is stronger?

I have in the past. Right now, no, since my goal is to spend as little time on the screens as possible, so I'm not even there watching the trade to make that decision. I'll often go to bed with entry orders sitting in the market and wake up to find out one of them was filled and closed. 

I might do something like that in the future again but for now, I'm pretty busy outside of trading so just trying to keep it simple and eliminate discretion everywhere but the entry.
I should have added that commissions are very difficult to overcome intraday. Unless you are able to get rebates vs paying commissions.
What you are referring to is noise vs signal. This is why intraday is very hard. Not impossible, but not easy. Given the substantial amount of noise, filtering through that to identify a proper signal for either continuation or reversal is quite difficult. 

Trading over multiple days/weeks is much easier, but also not easy. Trends can run for long periods of time (ie look at the long run gold had).
Don't have Claude (or any LLM) do statistical testing. Have it write software that does statistical testing, then have another LLM test and validate the software. (or just use an already backtester like vectorbt.) 

LLMs are nondeterministic. You do not want them to do direct statistical analysis.
That makes sense as trading is extremely personal. I think Adam Grimes does something similar to you in terms of targets. Do you apply the "veto" idea to your exits at all or is it just for entries? For example, holding the position for a higher ATR multiple when the narrative for the trade idea is stronger?
It is arbitrary, and yet it still outperforms other exit methods in the long run in all my tests, including more “sophisticated” exits based on structure and price action. 

If it’s arbitrary, but tests well and reduce decision making, I don’t view the fact that it is arbitrary as an inherent negative.
But isn't that kind of arbitrary? Forcing the ATR multiple you want out of the market based on your entry price?
it's possible to find a mechanical edge, however it's of course extremely difficult to do so. it's also good to keep in mind that a simple 52% win rate strategy with a 1:1 RR could return tens of millions if the edge holds true. with a 60% win rate, you'd easily become a billionaire in less than a decade and officially be one of, if not the best trader of all time.
Stops and targets are mechanical and based on fixed ATR multiples
Is your profit target mechanical or discretionary too? I am so far using a trailing moving average but want an ability to take profits into strength. The only problem is the profit into strength part feels discretionary.
A strategy cannot be entirely mechanically executed by a human, its just not possible. What you should be focusing on is risk management and trade management. You have to know your entry and exit before the trade is even placed. Its more like, if price reaches X, then i will do Y.  Also don't fall into the trap of being a fortune teller i.e price is gonna hit X, then it's gonna Y, then it'll Z.
You said FULLY mechanical. If you seriously think about it, it's not realistic. You basically want the goose that lays a golden egg. Doesn't everyone?
I've found the best results strategies that sits very close to fully mechanical, but still requires me to "approve" or "veto" trade ideas. Fully defined setups/entries/exits, I just use discretion to filter them. 

Too mechanical, and I lose the "intangible" part of the edge that I can't define, that's rooted in experience and a subconscious read of market context. I've never found a backtest that does as well my live performance when I actively filter trade ideas. If I get five signals, I might pick one out of those five. 

But too much discretion, and I am prone to human error. I want to be involved as little as possible when it comes to actual execution and whether a valid signal is there
I trade a mechanical system but it seems there’s always a bit of discretion when there’s a human involved. I guess you could argue that you could add any discretionary item to the mechanical list but not sure. 

I have been trading futures for 6 years. I don’t make a living doing it but had my most successful year this year. 5 winning months making about 1,700 each. It’s ok but honestly I’ve been at this for só long I was expecting to be doing this full time by now. 

Also I blew the account last month after having a major life change. Kinda second guessing it all right now and wondering if i should focus on something else to provide for my family or if im close. 

I’m not interested in feed
Kind of  both for me because I trade price action but my setup is the same. I wait for a rejection at a key level and play the reversal but like someone said already, my brain will try to "create" those set ups when watching the price action live. It might seem like volume just came in or something and I'll take the entry but be wrong. And then oh boy, the "i got get my loss back and some" is what always kills me.
I've been chasing that for years, but the more quantitative testing on historical data I do in Claude against any strategy, the less likely in looks like it's possible. If someone has a mechanical system that works, that's awesome, I'm rooting for you.   
I think the main issue is that the forces that actually move price (the 'institutional' traders, in whatever form that may be) play the game differently then you or I. They are constantly getting in and out of positions by filling large trades over a period of time, or hedging at key areas to try to stay neutral or positive. We are trying to find sharp reversal or continuation patterns on a system that is moving more like an orbit or wave.
Not sure if it’s the way I process information but I do a lot better without strategy rules and use general guidelines.

With rules I would sometimes force a trade just because it fit the rules. Without rules I’m not looking for any set-ups but waiting for a set-up. Sounds similar but made a big difference in my trading.

Only rule I have is a daily loss limit.
Is it fully mechanical then or do you decide that on the fly, Where do you set stop and TP ?  
Are you focusing on one market?
i run a mostly mechanical setup but there's always that tiny voice that says "nah not this time" and i override it. that's where i lose money

  
the rules are simple. wait for the 15min to close above the 9ema, volume spike, enter on the retest. works like 65% of the time. problem is i get bored and start seeing patterns that aren't there

  
discretion is the trap disguised as skill. every time i trust my gut over the checklist i end up revenge trading at 2pm wondering what happened. if you can actually stick to mechanical you're already ahead of 90% of traders

title: Bạn sẽ ưu tiên duy trì chiến lược cơ học hay linh hoạt theo điều kiện thị trường?
text:
[Tranh luận thực chiến] Bạn sẽ ưu tiên duy trì chiến lược cơ học hay linh hoạt theo điều kiện thị trường?
- Góc nhìn A: Chiến lược cơ học giúp loại bỏ cảm xúc, giảm rủi ro do quyết định sai lầm và tăng tính nhất quán, nhưng nếu thị trường thay đổi, hệ thống có thể bị phá vỡ
- Góc nhìn B: Thị trường luôn biến động, các yếu tố không thể dự đoán; một chiến lược hoàn toàn cơ học dễ bị lỗi khi điều kiện thay đổi, vì vậy cần sự linh hoạt và can thiệp chủ quan
- Điểm mù cả hai phía chưa nói: Tầm quan trọng của việc kiểm tra liên tục và điều chỉnh chiến lược khi dữ liệu mới xuất hiện
- Lưu ý thiên kiến sống sót: Người có lệnh thắng thường lên tiếng nhiều hơn người đã cháy tài khoản.
Bạn nghiêng về hướng nào? Bỏ phiếu ở poll bên dưới (kết quả tổng hợp sau 48 giờ).
